items.question: The Spanish Heir (What If Carlos II had a son?)
human_answers: I'm very interested to see how the Habsburgs continue to manage their Mediterranean and American possessions. It might be too much to hope for, but perhaps if the final decades of his reign are less frantic, he might be a little more relaxed and not outlaw the use of Nahuatl and Quechua within the administration of the American colonies. Beyond that, continuing spanish rivalry with France will be interesting- I'd assume if Spain can get it's act together they'll be looking for a return of the franche comté. But as they're not as much of a land power as Austria, they might end up losing Belgium to France. Corsica and Tuscany are also up for grabs this century, which could confirm them as masters of all Italy. In the Mediterranean, Spanish support might lead to a longer lasting Catholic Morea, whether under the Venetians or under the Spanish themselves- and given how much the spanish the like Catholicism, it might scare the orthodox within the ottoman empire into closer association with the ottoman state. Austrian-ottoman wars in the beginning of the 18th century will be altered should the Spanish coordinate with their cousins by sea- Crete, Cyprus and even Rhodes could be targets here. The age of dynastic partitions is mainly over, but one more might just be on the cards- either Castile and the colonies Vs Aragon and the Mediterranean, or Spain and the colonies Vs Italy and the Mediterranean.

Carlos II's heir would however have to face the quandary his kingdom is confronted to as it was during Carlos II's reign that the decline of Spain truly began. He would however rely on the old age of Louis XIV when he will be of age to rule, which could be helpful as France remains a powerful rival and neighbour (and I spoke of it as a Frenchman).

I: The Habsburg Miracles The Battle of Vienna (1683) ​ On September 8, 1683, the nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived in Vienna. On this holy day, priests, citizens, and soldiers alike poured into the churches of Vienna or failing that, their steps, and prayed. For unlike any previous nativity, this one had been one that many expected to live to see. For two months, Vienna had been surrounded by more than 150,000 Turkish soldiers commanded by the Grand Vizier, Kara Mustafa, Pasha, himself. This mighty host had cut off Vienna entirely from the rest of the Christian world and bombarded it daily while the Ottoman trenches steadily advanced upon the city. The Austrian army and band of citizens that had been left behind by their frightened Emperor Leopold numbered less than 20,000. Their situation was desperate and even their stalwart garrison commander, Ernst Rudiger von Starhemberg, could sense that the city would not survive much longer, and once the Ottomans broke through its walls everyone knew that only a bloody execution awaited every one of them. In the grips of this terrible situation, Starhemberg and the defenders of Vienna could do nothing more than pray for deliverance from the Blessed Virgin Mary. That same Wednesday night those prayers were answered when the daily signal rockets of Vienna were answered by five rockets from Kahlenberg Hill in the west. Those five brilliant flashes signaled that the relief that Vienna had long-awaited and desperately needed was presently on its way. However, on Thursday, the only banners that waved in the fields around Vienna were the banners of the Ottomans and the soldiers beneath those banners remained in place, not diverted to fight some other foe. Of greatest concern, the cannonades against Vienna slackened, which only ever happened when the Ottomans were preparing a direct attack on the city. That afternoon, with the western horizon still devoid of signs of Christendom, an explosion rocked the western defenses of Vienna when a mine cratered part of Lobl Bastion. Soon after, hundreds of Ottoman soldiers charged up the slope toward Vienna's walls to wrench Lobl Bastion out of the defenders' hands. Starhemberg's expectation of this attack meant that the breach in Lobl's wall had been stuffed with Austrian soldiers. Even after close to sixty days of unending and horrific investment, the Austrians stood strong and drove back the Ottomans twice. The toll that the Austrians inflicted on their attacks was so severe that the Grand Vizier declined sending the third assault. Afterward, Starhemberg quickly organized the repairing and retrenchment of the outer defenses of Vienna. Additionally, Starhemberg backed up these fortifications with chains and barricades in the streets and homes behind the walls. Whether the signals of the day before were true precursors to a timely relief or not, Starhemberg had no intention of surrendering Austria's capital to the enemy. Death was a more palatable alternative. Those signals had not been for naught. A relief army had been formed and was in fact on its way. For the previous two months, just a mere 20,000 Imperial soldiers had remained within touching distance of Vienna to provide the vague suggestion of relief. But over the last weeks of August, that 20,000 men had been dramatically increased to create a real army. First, came 11,000 Bavarians under the personal command of the twenty-one-year-old Elector Maximilian II Emanuel. Unlike any other contingent, even the Emperor's own soldiers, Max Emanuel and his Bavarians had not demanded some incredible subsidy upfront or alternative reward to come to the aid of Vienna. The money could wait until Austria was not in the grips of catastrophe. For now, all Max Emanuel and the Bavarians required was an opportunity to demonstrate their bravery and prove their honor by saving the beleaguered city of Vienna. Shortly after the Bavarians arrived came an army of 6,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry from the Franconian and Swabian Circles. They had only come after weeks of careful negotiation between Emperor Leopold and the Circles, which ended with Emperor Leopold agreeing to pay them a large sum for their services. Next, came 7,000 foot and 2,000 horse of Saxony, who like the Bavarians were commanded by their ruler, Elector Johann Georg IV. While the Bavarians brought with them an impressive train of field artillery, the Saxons brought an essential set of light and mobile artillery pieces. Finally, some smaller units of Germans such as that of Julius Franz of Saxony-Lauenberg added to the army. The last piece of this army was 24,000 Polish footmen and hussars led by King Jan III Sobieski. This eastern army outdid the contribution of any single Imperial prince, even exceeding the army of Emperor Leopold himself. And this number was not even all of it. Some days behind the Poles lagged thousands of the Lithuanian subjects of King Jan III. Bringing this considerable army away from the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and then all the way to the Danube had left the Commonwealth itself practically defenseless. In fact, the only defense that King Jan III could offer was a stern warning and a threat of devastating retaliation against the Ottoman partisan Imre Thokoly if he attacked the Commonwealth in the King's absence. However, putting his home in danger was without a doubt necessary to give Christendom a chance to save Vienna. Without the Poles, the Imperial army counted only 50,000 men whereas, with them, the Christians numbered close to 75,000 soldiers. Although this final number was just half that of the Ottomans, it was far better than being only a third. With a King and two Imperial Electors holding commands within this great Christian army, the threat of splintered focus and disorganized tactics was high. Although Emperor Leopold was technically superior to each of them as the Holy Roman Emperor, his previous flight from Vienna had proven that the battlefield was not where his talents lay. Fortunately, the man who Emperor Leopold gave command of his soldiers to, Duke Charles V of Lorraine, proved to be the perfect individual to navigate this multinational army's complicated hierarchy. As the exiled ruler of an occupied duchy Charles of Lorraine's only vocation for the past decade had been being an Imperial general. Through this experience managing the Austrian army's diverse officer corps, Charles of Lorraine learned how to bring an army together around a singular goal through personally connecting with each and every commander of importance. Whereas others were brash and offensive or deferential and meek, Charles of Lorraine was straightforward and easy-going, which was a welcomed ideal among soldiers and commanders alike. Quickly, Charles of Lorraine gained the confidence of the Christian army's generals and bound them to the goal of rescuing Vienna above all else. Under Charles of Lorraine's guidance, Jan Sobieski, Max Emanuel, and Johann Georg all agreed to ignore Emperor Leopold's directive that the relief army should take a longer approach through the gentle grounds to the southwest of Vienna. Instead, in their eagerness to save Vienna, the relief army determined to reach the city as quickly as possible by taking the shortest path across the rocky outcrop of the Wienerwald. With all appropriate haste, the relief army soon cut its way through the forest to Vienna's northwest and then crossed the Danube dangerously close to the Ottoman outriders. By September 8, the army had made its way to Tulln, just 22 miles from Vienna, and was readying its final approach toward Vienna. That night they sent off the signal rockets to inform Vienna of their coming and inspire just a few more days of resistance from the city. When the relief army finally entered the Wienerwald on September 9, it was confronted by an unruly wilderness that had grown out of hand since the Habsburg Emperors had denied the forest to anyone but themselves. As a consequence, the relief army lost its cohesion as it filtered through the forest and up its steep slopes. No man found comfort as he marched or rode through the crowded woods and its sprawling undergrowth, all the while thoughts of a terrible battle hung over him. To make matters worse, a German scouting party spotted Ottomans holding part of the ridgeline in the way of the army's approach. The Ottomans, however, lacked the foresight to either fortify or sufficiently man that ridgeline. This allowed the Christians to pounce on the Ottoman position between dawn on September 11 and wrest control of the ridgeline before the Ottomans could realize their mistake. Yet this victory was not complete as several Ottomans managed to escape from the skirmish and flee back to the main camp where they made the Grand Vizier aware of the relief army's imminent approach. Ottoman scouts had already revealed the relief army to the Grand Vizier two days prior to this attack on the ridge. However, the survivors of the attack were able to confirm the whereabouts of the relief army and its size, which verified the Ottoman belief that the relief army intended to come straight at them from the west and that no attack should be expected from the south where the patrols had still not encountered any Christian soldiers. The narrow geography of the Wienerwald meant that the best avenue for an attack was straight at the center of the Ottoman position. This position could be defended by a series of mannered ridges, hills, and villages. Although the Grand Vizier decided against enhancing the natural defenses provided by the topography with either trenches or palisades, the series of obstacles still presented a formidable challenge. The Christians would have to funnel themselves into multiple zones of fire and if the Ottomans held their ground then it would be a slaughter. Another set of obstacles and an even greater challenge for the Christian army would have to be overcome before they could even reach the Ottoman defenses. After the morning's victory, the Christians were able to occupy the ridge of Kalhenburg and look down toward Vienna. The maps had led them to believe that between that ridge and Vienna lay gentle slopes and clear ploughed fields. Instead, the rocky and uneven ground that had begrudged them in the Wienerwald continued on all the way to the edge of Vienna. The lines that separated the fields were not low wooden fences but haphazard stone walls and thick hedgerows that could not easily be traversed. These demarcations enclosed not open fields of crops but thick and twisted vines of unharvested grapes. Further complicating this approach was a set of deep ravines, small streams, and some scattered villages. Any of these alone was an impediment, but all of them together formed a veritable wall against an assault. As the Christians piloted this difficult terrain they would be easy targets for the Ottoman cannons and muskets. The cavalrymen high up on their horses would be particularly exposed as they slowly negotiated the convoluted ground. All in all, the Christians would have no hope of sending in straight lines of pikemen and musketeers or charging forth coherent blocks of horsemen. Instead, the Christians would have to advance slowly and carefully across the difficult ground and under heavy fire before throwing themselves against prepared defenses and ready defenders. In the face of this adversity, the Christians did not cower. They had come all this way to save Vienna and they would do their damnedest to try, even with so much going against them. However, the Christians' willingness to push on was not the result of confidence or of faith. Many Christian soldiers spent that night sleepless and unable to stomach any food. Even Charles of Lorraine was nervous on the precipice of this battle. They all understood that the likelihood of their victory was low and believed that many of their souls would depart on the morrow. It would be a red day, all they could do was hope it would not be a black day too. On Sunday, September 12, 1683, the great battle for Vienna began when hundreds of Ottoman skirmishers began climbing up the slope toward Kalhenburg and opened fire on the Christian army at around 5 am. With men dropping left and right, the Christians could not hold still and simply return fire. Instead, the Saxon infantrymen abandoned their positions and drove down the hill toward the Ottomans. The whole left flank of the Christian army joined the Saxons in this counterattack that swept away the eastern skirmishers. Although the first Ottoman attack was thrown back, the left flank of the Christian army had placed itself well ahead of the rest of the army in doing so, which left it vulnerable to an Ottoman counterattack. Charles of Lorraine took quick notice of the danger and ordered the left to slow its advance while the rest of the Christian army was ordered to catch up. Although the Saxons had dragged the rest of the army out of its strong positions along the ridge, the earlier success had inspired the men with confidence and even Charles of Lorraine could feel something. The order for a general attack was given. As the Christians crowded around the Ottoman stronghold of Nussberg, they cried out "Ave Maria!" and the Ottomans threw back "Allah, Allah Akbar!" These screams and shouts were drowned out by the overwhelming sound of muskets firing, cannons blasting, and swords clattering. The fighting was vicious and uncertain. But at that particular spot, the Christians found themselves more numerous than the Ottomans and steadily overcame their Ottoman forest. Of great importance were the Saxon light cannons that had been successfully dragged down the slope to directly fire into the Ottoman formations. Within the Ottoman camp, the Grand Vizier was well-aware of the unfolding battle and committed his reserve to saving Nussberg and holding back the Christians. However, the Grand Vizier failed to organize a larger reinforcement from other parts of the army because he could not coordinate with the various pashas and Tatar chiefs. In contrast, even with the dreadful terrain and multinational nature of the army, Charles of Lorraine had maintained decent lines and formations. Close to noon, Johann Georg's cavalry was unleashed on the Ottoman sipahis, which allowed the Saxon infantrymen to wrest Nussberg away from the Ottomans. Still, the Saxons had to fight the Ottomans for each and every house in that village. the continuance of this attack faltered as the Saxons once more overextended themselves in the chase. But once the Christians regrouped they renewed their attack and took the next Ottoman stronghold in front of them. At this point, Charles of Lorraine called for the army to hold to avoid another overextension. He needed to ensure that the army did not lose its cohesion and under the hot summer sun, Charles of Lorraine was worried about his soldiers suffering from exhaustion and thirst. This pause allowed the thousands of Polish cavalry to make their way down the slopes from the Wienerwald and toward the southern edge of the Ottoman position. With the Christian army having successfully made it down the slopes and having already broken one Ottoman position, the Christians finally found themselves at the advantage. Even though the Ottoman army as a whole was larger than the Christian one, on those fields to the west of Vienna, the Christians were superior in number. And now that they had made it down the slope, those numbers could be fully deployed against the Ottomans. Both Charles of Lorraine and Jan Sobieski could feel this shift. To the northeast, Charles of Lorraine asked the German commanders if they wished to push on or whether they should delay the battle to the next day. To the south, Jan Sobieski asked his own commanders the same question. In both councils, the answer was the same: March on. With this order shouted out, the Christians moved forward once again and pushed up to the remaining positions. In the north, the Imperial soldiers led by the Bavarians and Saxons assaulted the Ottoman formations and after an hour and a half, conquered them. All the enemies within them were slaughtered. To the south, the Poles sent a forlorn hope forth to test the Ottoman positions. Although this lonesome company was mauled by the far more numerous Ottomans, their charge still shook the Ottomans just enough for Jan Sobieski to order the entirety of his hussars and the rest of the cavalry to charge the Ottomans. When the Poles bore down on them, the Ottomans did not present themselves as the vicious conquerors of Constantinople. Instead, demoralized by the morning and afternoon's travails, the Ottomans were a disorderly mess that lacked the spirit and discipline necessary to hold against a cavalry charge. The Poles punched through the Ottomans and began to cut them to pieces. Quickly, the Ottomans lost the last of their courage and began to flee. Meanwhile, the Germans to the north continued to stomp over the Ottomans in front of them. Within the hour, the Ottoman army was broken and sent into flight. The citizens of Vienna rejoiced when Charles of Lorraine's official messenger pronounced that "Vienna was relieved". Thousands exited their homes and cried out in jubilation in the streets while others exited the city to set their eyes on their glorious saviours. Everywhere music played and tears of joy and relief painted faces. Although the army remained on alert for the rest of the night in case the Ottomans came back, all knew that no such thing would happen. By some miracle of God, an army of fewer than 75,000 men had secured a true and complete victory over an army of more than 150,000. Vienna was saved and the Ottomans were shattered [1] . While this miracle on the Danube saved Emperor Leopold from suffering the same ignominy of losing Vienna as his ancestor Emperor Frederick III, it was not the only miracle to bless the House of Habsburg on that day. More than a thousand miles away in the heart of Spain at the Royal Alcazar of Madrid, another miracle was delivered to the Habsburgs. There, after twelve hours of screaming and crying, Queen Marie Louise of Spain gave birth to the long-awaited first child of King Carlos II of Spain [2] . Better yet, she gave birth to a son who could inherit the many crowns of Spain without any dispute. Thus, Marie Louise ended nearly two decades of uncertainty over who would next possess the crown of Spain. Just as the victory over the Ottomans was celebrated by all within Vienna, the birth of a son, a crown prince, was celebrated by all within Madrid. To them, there could be no greater miracle than that which saved them from a dozen European rulers laying claim to some piece of the Spanish empire once the sickly King Carlos II's heart finally gave out. Thus, both halves of the Habsburg dynasty were saved on the fateful day of September 12, 1683. [1] This is a retelling of the historical relief of Vienna. There is no alteration to make note of. [2] This is the Point of Divergence, Marie Louise produces an heir. There is at least one rumored pregnancy for Marie Louise during her marriage to Carlos II. Unlike the rumored pregnancies of her successor Maria Anna of Neuburg, this rumored pregnancy was taken seriously and not believed to be completely chimerical. One reason for that difference in reactions was that although Carlos II was never conventionally healthy, he was far more relatively healthy while married to Marie Louise. During this time, the only believed issue with conception was his premature ejaculation. Later, when married to Maria Anna, Carlos II was suffering from increasing health issues including atrophy. Here, the suggestion is that Carlos II and Marie Louise manage to get lucky and overcome his premature ejaculation to produce an heir. Alternatively, you are welcome to believe that Marie Louise found another partner. Or even that this is a legitimate miracle from God. Either way, she has produced a child whom Spain will accept as the heir.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling and dynastic plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly anchors the scenario in a surviving legitimate son of Carlos II and plausibly reasons through succession, regency, legitimacy, and Habsburg continuity without treating the historical Bourbon succession as inevitable.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or misunderstands the premise; still assumes the War of the Spanish Succession proceeds unchanged or Carlos II dies heirless.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges a son but gives little attention to legitimacy, age, regency, health, or acceptance by Spanish and European elites.
criteria.5-6: Explains that a legitimate heir likely prevents or delays the 1701 Bourbon accession, with some plausible discussion of minority rule or factional politics.
criteria.7-8: Develops a credible succession path, including regency, court factions, Habsburg alliances, and likely recognition or resistance by France, Austria, and other powers.
criteria.9-10: Integrates dynastic law, elite acceptance, timing of birth and majority, Habsburg health concerns, and European diplomatic reactions into a coherent altered succession settlement.

criteria.name: European balance-of-power consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage and causal treatment of how a Spanish Habsburg heir affects France, Austria, Britain, the Dutch Republic, Italy, the Low Countries, and the likelihood, timing, or form of major wars.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful European geopolitical consequences or makes claims disconnected from the altered succession.
criteria.3-4: Mentions France or Austria in passing but treats the European balance of power superficially or anachronistically.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that the War of the Spanish Succession is likely avoided, delayed, or transformed and notes some effects on France, Austria, Britain, or the Dutch.
criteria.7-8: Traces multiple knock-on effects: French rivalry, Austrian Habsburg coordination, British/Dutch maritime interests, Italian territories, and the Spanish Netherlands.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced map of alternative conflicts and settlements, including possible French pressure on Belgium/Franche-Comté, Austrian-Spanish coordination, British naval aims, and shifting Italian-Mediterranean contests.

criteria.name: Imperial, colonial, and administrative mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer considers Spain’s American empire, fiscal-military capacity, administrative reform, colonial languages and elites, trade, and whether avoiding succession crisis changes or fails to change Spanish decline.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the Spanish empire and assumes Spain simply becomes strong or weak without mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions colonies or wealth vaguely but does not connect them to administration, finance, or imperial governance.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that avoiding a succession war may preserve resources while Spain still faces structural fiscal, military, and administrative problems.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible reforms or continuities in the Americas, taxation, trade regulation, local elites, language policy, and the limits of Habsburg governance.
criteria.9-10: Balances avoided wartime devastation with deep structural constraints, comparing likely Habsburg trajectories to Bourbon reforms and showing specific colonial, fiscal, and administrative consequences.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence across the 18th century
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer builds a sustained, logically connected chain from Carlos II’s heir through mid- and late-18th-century outcomes rather than listing isolated possibilities.
criteria.1-2: Gives disconnected speculation with no temporal chain or clear causal links.
criteria.3-4: Provides a short-term change only, with little sense of how later decades are affected.
criteria.5-6: Connects the altered succession to several later developments, though some links are underexplained or overly linear.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a coherent sequence involving succession, diplomacy, wars, reforms, colonial policy, and Mediterranean or Atlantic competition over decades.
criteria.9-10: Constructs a robust long-range scenario with feedback loops, contingencies, institutional inertia, rival state responses, and plausible divergence points through much of the 18th century.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes while avoiding internal contradictions, deterministic overclaims, and conflicts with known historical constraints.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but implausible assertions, contradicts itself, or ignores basic historical chronology and constraints.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but includes major overclaims, contradictions, or unsupported inevitabilities.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible and mostly consistent, with some hedging and recognition that outcomes such as war, reform, or partition remain uncertain.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates probable from possible developments, flags key contingencies, and avoids contradictions about dynastic succession, alliances, and imperial capacity.
criteria.9-10: Consistently calibrated, historically constrained, and internally coherent; presents alternative branches where appropriate without losing causal focus.

If Carlos II of Spain had a legitimate surviving son, the most immediate effect would be that the War of the Spanish Succession probably would not happen in the form it did, and perhaps not at all.

The crisis of 1700 existed because Carlos II died childless and the Spanish monarchy was enormous: Spain, Spanish America, the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, Naples, Sicily, Sardinia, and other possessions. France wanted the inheritance for the Bourbon Philip of Anjou; Austria wanted it for the Habsburg Archduke Charles; Britain and the Dutch Republic mainly wanted to prevent either France or Austria from becoming too dominant. A legitimate Spanish heir would remove the strongest legal excuse for partition or foreign succession.

The likely result would be the continuation of a Spanish Habsburg line. If the son were still a minor when Carlos II died, Spain would probably be ruled by a regency, and that regency would become the object of intense French, Austrian, papal, and Spanish factional pressure. But foreign powers would have found it much harder to justify replacing a living legitimate prince. Britain and the Dutch might even have preferred recognizing him, because a separate Spain under its own king was safer than Spain being absorbed into the orbit of either Versailles or Vienna.

So Spain would probably keep its empire intact at first. There would likely be no Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, meaning Britain probably would not receive Gibraltar and Minorca in that context, Austria would not receive the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, Naples, or Sardinia from Spain, and the Bourbon dynasty would not take the Spanish throne. The political map of eighteenth-century Europe would look very different.

But this does not mean Spain would suddenly recover its former greatness. A child of Carlos II might well have been physically weak or politically dependent, given the inbreeding and institutional decay of the late Spanish Habsburg monarchy. Even with a clear heir, Spain still faced deep fiscal weakness, military decline, regional privileges that limited central control, dependence on foreign finance, and administrative stagnation. The monarchy might survive, but it would still need reform.

One important difference is that the Bourbon centralizing reforms probably would not occur, or would occur much more slowly. Philip V and his successors imposed major changes after the War of the Spanish Succession, especially the Nueva Planta decrees, which reduced the autonomy of the Crown of Aragon and made Spain more centralized on a French model. Under a continued Spanish Habsburg line, Spain would likely remain more composite and decentralized, with Castile, Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, and other territories retaining more of their older institutions.

France would benefit indirectly. Without the long War of the Spanish Succession, Louis XIV’s France would avoid a hugely expensive and exhausting conflict. France might remain stronger in the early eighteenth century, though it would not gain a Bourbon Spain as an ally. Austria, meanwhile, would be weaker than in real history because it would not acquire the Spanish Netherlands and large parts of Italy. Britain would still be a rising naval and commercial power, but its Mediterranean position and its formal trading privileges in Spanish America might develop more slowly or through different wars and treaties.

The biggest uncertainty is the health and survival of the son. If Carlos II’s son died young, the succession crisis would simply be postponed, and Europe could still face a major war later. If he lived but was weak, Spain might become the arena for diplomatic domination by France or Austria. If he were capable and had strong ministers, Spain might achieve modest reform while preserving the Habsburg empire longer.

In short: a surviving son of Carlos II would probably prevent the Bourbon succession and likely avert the War of the Spanish Succession as we know it. Spain would remain Habsburg and keep more of its empire in the short term, but it would not automatically become powerful again. The eighteenth century would probably see a weaker Austria, a less exhausted France, a less centralized Spain, and a Britain that still rises—but without the same early gains from Utrecht.

A “wanked” but still semi-plausible George W. Bush presidency would probably require three big divergences: 9/11 is prevented or greatly reduced, Iraq is avoided, and the 2008 financial crisis is softened. With those changes, Bush could plausibly leave office as a popular center-right reform president rather than as one defined by war, Katrina, and recession.

The cleanest point of divergence is summer 2001. The CIA and FBI cooperate better after the Phoenix memo, the Moussaoui arrest is handled more aggressively, and the August 6 Presidential Daily Brief triggers a serious interagency review. Two or three of the hijackers are detained on immigration or material-support grounds, the plot collapses, and the public later learns that the administration helped stop a major al-Qaeda attack. Bush does not get the enormous post-9/11 rally effect, but he also avoids the catastrophic consequences of the War on Terror.

Without 9/11, there is no invasion of Afghanistan and no Iraq War. Bush still pursues a hawkish foreign policy, but it is more Clinton/Bush Sr.-style: sanctions, intelligence cooperation, drone and special forces strikes, pressure on Saddam Hussein, and expanded homeland security. The neoconservatives remain influential, but they never get the political opening needed for a full-scale Iraq invasion. This alone saves trillions of dollars, avoids thousands of American deaths, prevents the Abu Ghraib and WMD-intelligence scandals, and keeps U.S. prestige much higher.

Domestically, Bush governs closer to the image he campaigned on in 2000: “compassionate conservatism.” He still passes tax cuts, but in a more restrained version because there is no wartime emergency politics. No Child Left Behind passes with bipartisan support and is later modified rather than becoming a symbol of federal overreach. Medicare Part D still happens, but with stronger cost controls and perhaps permission for Medicare to negotiate some drug prices. Bush also has more room to push immigration reform, and with no Iraq poisoning the political climate, a McCain-Kennedy-style compromise might pass around 2005–06.

The other major improvement is Katrina. In this timeline, Bush appoints a more competent FEMA leadership or reacts faster when the storm hits. Federal troops and relief supplies arrive sooner, the administration is visibly engaged, and Bush avoids the “heck of a job, Brownie” moment becoming a symbol of detachment. Katrina is still a disaster, but not a presidency-defining disgrace.

Finally, the housing bubble and financial crisis need to be reduced. This is the hardest part, because many causes predate Bush and were global. But a favorable Bush timeline could have him appoint regulators who take mortgage fraud, subprime lending, and derivatives risk more seriously by 2004–05. The SEC does not loosen leverage rules as much, Fannie and Freddie are reined in earlier, and the Fed raises rates or uses regulatory tools more aggressively against reckless lending. The result is still a recession in 2007–08, but more like a sharp housing correction than a global financial meltdown.

In this version, Bush leaves office in January 2009 with a mixed but respectable record: tax cuts, education reform, Medicare expansion, immigration reform, no Iraq War, a foiled al-Qaeda attack, and a milder recession. Conservatives remember him as the president who restored Republican dominance after Clinton; moderates see him as a flawed but decent bipartisan conservative; liberals still dislike his tax policy, social conservatism, and deregulation, but he is not viewed as a disastrous president.

His approval rating might plausibly end around 50–60% instead of the low 30s. Historians would likely rank him somewhere in the upper-middle tier, perhaps comparable to Eisenhower in Republican memory but more controversial fiscally. The Republican Party would also look very different: less discredited by Iraq, less radicalized by the Obama backlash, and possibly more committed to Bush-style pro-immigration, business-friendly conservatism.

items.question: What If Best timeline for Catholicism
human_answers: As mentioned, this would be difficult without changing core doctrines. That basically requires the Schism to occur, and likely makes it difficult to avoid the Reformation. Here's a few thoughts though: A successful Crusade of Varna could lead to greater Catholic influence over the Balkans/southeastern Europe in place of the Ottomans. If there's enough pressure the Byzantines may be able to remain Eastern Catholic – this would be unpopular among the people, but foreign relations and actual successes by the Catholic powers in combatting the Ottomans may counteract this. Same goes for other newly liberated groups in the Balkans like the Bulgarians and Wallachians. For Russia, the best bet may be to have Poland-Lithuania successfully bring Russia under its influence, such as through a pretender like False Dmitri. This could lead to the imposition of Catholicism on Russia, which again would face resistance from the people, but depending on the level of Polish control could result in a Catholic Russia. Theoretically, the Reformation may be avoidable if Rome preemptively implements several of the reforms seen in OTL's Counter-Reformation and Council of Trent. This would alleviate most of Luther's early concerns, and may lead to later, more radical Reformers being far less influential. Of course, given that it was the Counter -Reformation, it doesn't seem likely that the Church would undergo these changes without Protestant pressure. The English Reformation, however, can pretty easily be undone just by changing some events in Tudor England. Maybe Arthur lives and Henry VIII never accedes, maybe Mary is born a male, maybe Henry VIII dies before his rejection of Rome. This in turn would make all of the major colonial powers Catholic, with the only exceptions being the Dutch and Scandinavians. If colonization goes similarly, this would make North America, Oceania, and likely other colonial possessions Catholic rather than Protestant.

But the thing is, the world around that Church would change too, and by it changing, so would to a degree the Church (by having to care about different things and facing different challenges) which may well render it unrecognizable. Much in the same way I can say (as a Catholic) the Church ontologically is the same as in the years 33 or 330, while still recognizing it looks and feels alien when superimposed to either of those Churches. So if we are to remain as close as you want, I guess EdwardRex's point works (with some luck, as it's easier to prevent Anglicanism than to prevent the rise of Protestantism), plus a different Italian unification that leaves a sizable Papal States not just existing, but also having a solid level of influence in geopolitics. Catholic Japan is objectively hard, go look at how lucky it was for the Philippines to end up how they did and then multiply it for Japan to experience something similar. As for Africa, I don't see any easy way out, there's a very unpalatable option in the form of continued colonialism I guess but I'd say it's not the best timeline for most anybody involved.

That's absolutely fair, the Church would feel very foreign to a modern layman. As a Catholic myself, learning about early Church history made me realize how alien it feels, even if it isn't so far off doctrinally. I should have said that, ideally, the Church doesn't compromise on its beliefs to prevent a division (e.g. remaining papist in a "no Schism of 1054" scenario, which would basically require divine intervention to overcome logistical problems). The question is, is preventing Anglicanism going to change all that much overall? Perhaps if you couple that with a more successful counter-reformation you could go far without preventing the rise of Protestantism altogether, which has massive ramifications for the French Wars of Religion and the Thirty Years' War. As for Italian unification, I think that a "best-case scenario" for the Church in this sense means dampening liberalism, and a great way to do that is to avoid the American and French revolutions, which therefore make nationalism a lot slower and less prominent, so whether Italy unifies is unlikely. I used Catholic Japan as an example, but a better one would be a Catholic Britain, which is much more likely and doesn't require a massive bloody unification war and shakeup of society. A Catholic Britain means that they would be exporting Catholicism rather than Protestantism to their colonies, which would likely cause a lot more people to be Catholics in the end. As for Africa, considering that there are a lot of Catholics in Africa as-is and that the main colonial powers are all Catholic, not much change is needed. Although I can imagine a world with no French revolution results in an extended colonization period.

I again agree with Evil Crusader, since depending on the Pod or the goal you want to achieve, yes they will get directly related developments, I give three practical examples : the first concerns a larger Patrimonium Petrii than Otl, this will technically mean that Rome is also politically more important at the regional level, but it will compromise its influence and image as an impartial actor at the international level, the second, instead of a cultural one, can be achieved with a Papacy that somehow manages to avoid everything that happens after the Avignon Captivity ( or with a more successful crusader movement ), maintaining its openness to foreign Pontiffs ( rather than being politically traumatized by all this in Otl ), It is by increasing the probability that the courts of Europe want to strengthen their relations with Rome, finally there is the third scenario that can lead to a weaker Papacy at the central level, but perhaps through the conciliar system it manages to reincorporate the various dissidents, in short anything can happen, but it is necessary to have an idea from which to start @Kellan Sullivan

Honestly, you don't really need to prevent the Schism of 1054. That particular schism as a singular historical event is majorly overblown in importance due to how the 12th century would play out. Frankly, schism didn't prevent cooperative efforts between East and West, even just a few scant years afterward. If you could somehow prevent the decline in relations between East and West during the 12th century, culminating in the 4th Crusade in 1204. Maybe if you could prevent the Roman contingent from breaking ranks with the Crusaders at Antioch and have Constantinople take possession of the city that could help a fair bit. Roman efforts to take the city from the Latins contributed a great deal to declining East-West relations during the century. Even better would be preventing the fall of Anatolia to the Turks entirely and thus butterflying the historical 1st Crusade entirely. Not that there would never be a crusade without the fall of Anatolia. There were talks of an armed pilgrimage to the Holy Land even before Manzikert.

A “best timeline” for Catholicism would probably not be one where the Church simply becomes more politically powerful. The strongest counterfactual timeline would be one where Catholicism remains doctrinally recognizable, avoids its biggest ruptures and scandals, reforms earlier, and becomes globally influential without coercion or colonial abuse.

In that timeline, the early Church still survives Roman persecution and becomes legal under Constantine, but it resists becoming too dependent on imperial power. Christianity spreads through preaching, charity, monasticism, hospitals, schools, and intellectual life, rather than through state pressure. The Church develops the creeds and biblical canon much as it did historically, but with a stronger early tradition of toleration toward Jews, pagans, and dissenters.

The first major improvement would be avoiding the permanent East–West Schism of 1054. A better settlement over papal primacy, the Filioque, and liturgical diversity could have preserved communion between Rome and Constantinople. The Pope might be recognized as a universal court of appeal and symbol of unity, while the Eastern patriarchs retain real autonomy. If the Fourth Crusade never sacks Constantinople in 1204, Catholic–Orthodox relations remain far healthier, and Christianity is stronger in the eastern Mediterranean.

The second major improvement would be earlier medieval reform. The Gregorian Reform still happens, but corruption, simony, nepotism, and clerical immorality are dealt with more consistently. The papacy remains spiritually respected rather than becoming too entangled in Italian politics. Crusading is either limited to defensive military action or redirected into diplomacy, pilgrimage protection, and aid to Eastern Christians, avoiding the worst atrocities and the long-term damage to Christian-Muslim relations.

The biggest turning point would be the 1500s. In the best Catholic timeline, the Church addresses indulgence abuse, clerical corruption, and calls for reform before Martin Luther’s protest becomes a permanent break. A council is called quickly in the 1510s or early 1520s, not decades later. Luther, Erasmus, and other reform-minded figures are engaged seriously rather than immediately condemned. The Church clarifies justification, grace, Scripture, and tradition in a way similar to later Catholic-Lutheran agreements, while allowing more vernacular Scripture, better preaching, and stronger lay catechesis. The result is that Protestantism may still exist as a reform movement, but Northern Europe does not permanently split from Rome. There are no Wars of Religion on the same scale, no Thirty Years’ War devastation, and Catholicism retains much more of Germany, Scandinavia, England, and the Low Countries.

In the age of exploration, the best timeline requires Catholic missions to separate themselves more sharply from imperial conquest. The Church would condemn slavery and forced conversion earlier and more forcefully, backing figures like Bartolomé de las Casas from the beginning. Missions in the Americas, Africa, India, China, and Japan would emphasize local languages, local clergy, and cultural adaptation. The Chinese Rites controversy would be resolved in favor of prudent inculturation, allowing Catholicism to grow much more deeply in China and East Asia. Indigenous peoples would still suffer from disease and conquest, but the Church’s moral record would be far stronger if it consistently opposed exploitation.

Another important change would be the Galileo affair. In the best timeline, Catholic authorities avoid making heliocentrism into a theological crisis. The Church treats scientific models as legitimate inquiries into creation and keeps Catholic universities at the center of astronomy, physics, medicine, and mathematics. This preserves Catholicism’s reputation as a patron of reason rather than allowing a lasting “science versus religion” narrative to form.

In the 1800s and 1900s, the Church would engage liberal democracy, religious liberty, and human rights earlier and less defensively. Instead of seeing modernity mostly as a threat, it would distinguish between anti-clerical secularism and legitimate political freedom. Catholic social teaching still develops, but sooner: workers’ rights, unions, anti-racism, anti-colonialism, and economic justice become major Catholic causes earlier. Vatican II either happens earlier or unfolds with less internal conflict, because liturgical renewal, biblical scholarship, ecumenism, and lay participation have already been developing organically.

The most important modern improvement would be the handling of sexual abuse and institutional secrecy. In the best timeline, bishops adopt strict transparency and mandatory reporting as soon as abuse becomes known, remove offenders permanently, cooperate with civil authorities, and prioritize victims over institutional reputation. This would preserve enormous moral credibility and prevent one of the worst crises in modern Catholic history.

By the 21st century, this best timeline leaves Catholicism as a more unified global communion: still centered on Rome, still sacramental and creedal, but less associated with coercion, corruption, anti-intellectualism, or cover-up. The Orthodox remain in communion or close to it; the Reformation becomes a reform within Catholicism rather than a permanent fracture; Catholicism is stronger in Northern Europe, the Middle East, China, Japan, Africa, and the Americas; and the Church is seen as a leading defender of education, science, human dignity, the poor, and peace.

So the “best timeline” for Catholicism is not Catholic world domination. It is a timeline of earlier reform, preserved Christian unity, cleaner governance, better relations with science, non-coercive missions, stronger defense of the oppressed, and far fewer scandals. That would give Catholicism both greater numbers and much greater moral authority.

While he was a male-line member of the House of Wittelsbach, Philip was the Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg (and his brother would become Elector Palatine after the death of their childless uncle) and Wittelsbach was mostly used for the Bavarian branch of the family, with the Palatine branches mostly using "Palatine-X" as their house name (like the Spanish Hapsburgs who used "of Austria" as their surname) Looking forward to see what will be Philip's religious education, although seeing as his father is Lutheran and his uncle would support protestant tutors he will probably be on the "low-key protestant" side of things. EDIT: Also will be interesting to see how the Palatine inheritance will work out on this TL, Philip the Contentious's older brother Otto-Henry became Elector Palatine in 1556 after their uncle, Frederick, died childless. And Otto-Henry would himself die childless in 1559 (he was married from 1529 to 1543, but no children were born, he was probably the one sterile since his wife had 11 children from a previous marriage). In OTL Philip died childless in the 1540s, meaning that the Electoral title passed to a cousin, but since in this TL he has children, I'm curious to see if there will be a personal union between England and the Palatinate or Mary will have a second son so they can divide the inheritance

For the last six years of her father's reign, Mary and Philip largely stayed out of court affairs, only returning for King Henry's last two marriages and Christmastide celebrations. While Mary's relationship with Kitty Howard was scarcely remarked upon before and after the unfortunate queen was executed, she and Catherine Parr had become close friends, with Catherine being godmother to Mary's third daughter, Mary just as Anna of Cleves was godmother to little Elizabeth. However, Mary's relationship with her father seemed to deteriorate as it was becoming quite clear that Henry was disappointed that he only had granddaughters. He even suggested that little Katherine should be raised in her aunt's household to make sure she didn't become as insolent as her namesake. Mary refused to speak to her father for a almost four months after that and it was only through Catherine Parr's intervention did Henry not go through with drawing up an act of succession that would skip over Mary and her daughters. When King Henry passed away in January 1547, Mary discovered she was pregnant again. Six months after her father's death, she gave birth to a son. She named him Philip after his father who greeted the birth of his son just as happily as he had the birth of his three daughters. There was some discussion over whether or not the boy would take his father's surname or his mother's as King Henry had decreed when Philip and Mary were first married. As his Uncle Edward's heir, some even wanted the boy to be raised somewhere else. Mary put her foot down, saying that if her husband's name was good enough for their daughters, it was good enough for her sons. She did not say a word about Phillip being taken from her. Of course, she hardly needed to as the Duke of Somerset, the Lady Elizabeth, Anna of Cleves and the Dowager Queen Catherine made it extremely clear to Edward, how utterly awful that would be. The boy-king himself wasn't too keen on the idea, considering he had never known his mother. In the end, Philip, Earl of Cambridge was known as Philip of Bedford and he would grow up in the Somerset household until he was six-years-old and started his formal schooling in Hatfield. Family tree: Philip, Duke of Somerset (b. 1503-) m. Mary of England (b. 1516). 1. Katherine of Somerset (b. 1540) 2. Elizabeth of Somerset (b. 1542). 3. Mary of Somerset (b. 1545). 4. Philip, Earl of Cambridge (b. 1547).
items.original_question: What if Princess Mary Tudor married Philip of Bavaria After a short courtship, King Henry announced that his daughter Lady Mary's engagement to Philip, Duke of Palatinate-Neuburg. Philip and Mary marry in early March in a small ceremony attended by the royal family and a few favored courtiers. Many expressed their displeasure at the match, chief among them the Imperial ambassador who wrote to the Holy Roman Emperor, lamenting that his poor cousin was now tied to a German Heathen who has no royal to speak of. The Earl of Hertford was similarly was not pleased with the marriage viewing any children Mary had as potential rivals to his nephew Prince Edward. Despite going through the process of getting a divorce from Anna of Cleves, King Henry remained on good terms with his son-in-law, even granting him the Duchy of Somerset once he abdicated his own duchy to his brother so he and Mary can stay in England. He was even happier to learn that Mary was pregnant with his first grandchild, requesting that the unborn son be named Henry for him. He was quite disappointed when on December 23, Mary had a daughter named Katherine instead.

Assuming you mean Princess Mary Tudor, Henry VIII’s daughter and the future Mary I, a marriage to Philip of Bavaria in the late 1530s or 1540s would probably have changed English politics less by making Mary “German” and more by preventing her later Spanish marriage to Philip II.

The biggest immediate effect would be diplomatic. Mary’s actual marriage to Philip of Spain in 1554 was deeply unpopular because many English people feared England would become subordinate to Spain and be dragged into Habsburg wars. A Bavarian or Wittelsbach husband would have been less threatening. Bavaria was important inside the Holy Roman Empire, but it was not a world power like Spain. So Mary’s marriage would likely have produced less anti-foreign panic, probably no Wyatt’s Rebellion in the same form, and less fear that England was becoming a Spanish satellite.

Religiously, Mary herself would almost certainly have remained Catholic. Her Catholicism came from her mother Catherine of Aragon, her own conscience, and her resistance to Henry VIII’s break with Rome. A Bavarian marriage would not have turned her Protestant. If she became queen, she would still likely try to restore Catholic worship and reconciliation with Rome. However, without the Spanish marriage, Catholic restoration might have looked less like a foreign project. Opposition to it may have been somewhat weaker, though Protestant resistance would still have existed. The Marian burnings might still have happened, because they were driven mainly by domestic religious policy, bishops, Parliament’s revival of heresy laws, and Mary’s own convictions, not simply by Spain.

The succession would be the crucial issue. If Mary and Philip of Bavaria had children, especially a son, Elizabeth would probably never have become queen. England might have passed into the hands of a Catholic Tudor-Wittelsbach heir. That would radically alter later history: no Elizabethan Religious Settlement as we know it, no Elizabethan Protestant identity in the same form, no Mary Queen of Scots crisis in the same way, and probably no Spanish Armada scenario as it happened. England might have remained officially Catholic for longer, though Protestantism would still have had strong support among parts of the nobility, clergy, merchants, and southeast England.

If Mary and Philip had no surviving children, the long-term result would be more limited. Mary might still become queen in 1553, restore Catholicism, and die without an heir, after which Elizabeth would still inherit. But Elizabeth’s reign would begin in a different diplomatic climate: England might not have been tied so closely to Spain, might not have entered Spain’s war against France, and therefore might have avoided or delayed the loss of Calais in 1558.

So the most likely broad outcome is this: Mary’s reign would have been less dominated by fear of Spanish influence, England might have avoided war with France and the loss of Calais, and Catholic restoration might have faced somewhat less nationalist opposition. But the truly transformative change would depend on children. A surviving child of Mary and Philip of Bavaria could have prevented Elizabeth I’s accession and changed the entire religious and dynastic direction of England.

items.question: What If Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible
human_answers: I suppose the first question is what is meant by apocrypha? Because it can mean different things and they're all different to address. Is it what many Protestants and Rabbinic Judaism call apocrypha? That is the additional books of the Old Testament that are instead considered Deuterocanon in Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy? At its core, these are books found in the LXX (Septuagint), but not found in the Masoretic text and are considered canonical texts for the majority of the Christian world. Removing the Protestant Masoretic preference resolves that part easily. Is it the broader Second Temple literature, often called Jewish Apocrypha? This is largely apocalyptic literature and includes things like Enoch, the somewhat related Jubilees, Esdras A (or III Ezra, or I Esdras...) , the Apocalypse of Esdra (IV Ezra/II Esdras), the various Baruchs, but also includes Wisdom literature like Psalms 151-155, Wisdom of Sirach, and the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs. Some of these were contained in LXX translations (Sirach, the Esdras, Psalms 151-155, etc), while others weren't (Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs, II Baruch, Enoch). This is a mixed bag for canonical status, some of them made it in due to being in existing Greek collections (the LXX), while others weren't. Enoch certainly saw a lot of respect in the early church, but it ultimately lost its status over time and only remained in Ethiopia; which itself has weird canon, the Ethiopic Bible includes Enoch and Jubilees before the Esdras, and also includes the 3 Books of Meqabyan (Ethiopic Maccabees), while disincluding the actual Books of Maccabees (and the Ethiopic books are not at all related, they aren't about martyrs at all in fact, and are almost certainly written in the Middle Ages in Ge'ez originally). A lot of these are interesting books that could have significant impact on theology, but most of them are written quite late too, which was a large part of why they weren't included in any canon; most were know pseudepigrapha even at the time. Then we have the New Testament apocrypha, which ranges from things like gnostic literature and known pseudepigrapha with little chance of incorporation to the antilegomena, many of which had good chance of inclusion. Those not included, but that could have been are the Gospel of the Hebrews (scholars think there's actually 3 different works under this title, and they're all lost), the Apocalypse of Peter, the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Epistle of Barnabas and the Didache. Worth stating is that the antilegomena weren't "removed," there was heavy debate early in Christianity of what was and wasn't canonical. Different churches used different books. Some were popular in one place, but unknown in others. Worth stating for the record: the Council of Nicea had NOTHING to do with canonical formation and this was still getting discussed for centuries after. The Church Father Jerome is one of the most important figures in the Old Testament canon development, he was highly influential in the West and was one of the main reasons for why the Catholic and Orthodox Deuterocanons are slightly different. As far as the New Testament, most of the Acts of the Apostyles genre were known pseudepigrapha and very clearly non-canonical even in content. They were popular literature and very clearly derived from the Greek novel tradition. Acts of Paul being one exception to this, it was deeply popular and some argued canonical, but in a canon that includes the Pastorals (and even the Deutero-Paulines), it just didn't fit with the theology of the Pauline letters (although I'd argue it fits quite well with the Authentic Pauline corpus). The Apocylpse of Peter wasn't actually well regarded by most priests and theologians though, but it was certainly popular. Its essentially an early Dante's Inferno. The Shepherd/Hermas, Barnabas (NOT the Gospel of Barnabas, which is a medieval forgery), and the Didache I think are the easiest bunch, although not entirely without problem. The Shepherd is deeply allegorical, but was known to not be apostolic (not insurmountable, as Hebrews made it in, but apostolic lineage was important) and has an arguably binitarian lean to it. Barnabas is also allegorical and also deeply anti-jewish. It is essentially saying that the Jews misread their own books, and this is what the Jewish laws really mean - a lot of these require some serious contortion, to say the least. The Didache is interesting since its the first book of the genre of "Church Orders," which are basically moral and litergical texts. In some ways, its an early version of the genre that would become the Anglican Book of Common Prayer. Some other possibilities are the Odes of Solomon, which are a Judeo-Christian work, likely from the Qumran community, with a pretty strong connection to the Johannine literature.

Another work to consider is the Ascension of Isaiah, a christian work written as a series of visions/prophecies of the prophet Isaiah. Also, the Book of Adam and Eve could become part of the Bible, it discusses what happens to Adam and Eve after Genesis, which is interesting. I doubt the distinction of a so-called "Thomasine" branch of anything, seeing as the gospel of Thomas is a late forgery, dating from the 2nd Century, and not originating from any known centers of Christianity claiming Thomasine origin, Kerala, Edessa or Bactria. The chance of the Didache becoming part of the Bible seems slight to me, seeing as its genre isnt really saying it should be, its just a how to book, thought to be directed to clergy. I would agree the best chance to expand is going to be the Apostolic fathers works: Letters of Ignatius, Polycarp, possibly Papias' work might make it in as a supplement to Acts of the Apostles.

Something to keep in mind, is that "canon" actually has different meanings. And what you mean by "canon" could have major implications on just how big it can get. To general Protestants, the Biblical Canon means that these are only 66 divinely inspired books, period, no more, no less (the familiar Protestant Canon). The Catholic teaching is a bit more nuanced. It states that there are at least 73 divinely inspired books (which make up the Catholic Canon). This does actual leave open the possibility that there are other books that could be divinely inspire but just are not included. That said, there are some individual books that have been rule as incompatible with canon & not divinely inspired. For most of the other Christian sects, the concept of canon is a bit "fuzzier." With many of the books falling into a category that could best be described as "potentially divinely inspired, but since it we see no problems with it we don't need to bother making any further determinations". Thus they are still included in the canon list.

Yes I am including those (potentially). It's a challenge though so it's more of a "would it be realistic" thing. And no real timeline, could be very early or very late. No, as long as there is a somewhat notable text that does consider them canonical. For instance 1 Enoch is not considered orthodox by the majority of Christians but there is at least one denomination that does consider it such. I see. That does make sense. Apparently a lot of stories that have become Christian folklore (of sorts) are from books like the Infancy Gospel that are not usually considered canon, but there are traces throughout art and popular imagination (and even in Islam). Some of the non-canonical Gospels and Acts for instance, additional pseudo-Pauline epistles (and letters by other figures). Could be a fairly small but still notable enough to make it into the historical record and maybe persist as a niche sect.

AHC: Have a Christian or Post-Christian religion incorporate as many "apocrypha" into its canon as possible

The definition of "apocrypha" obviously varies across denomination, e.g. 1 Enoch is canon according to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church but not any other major denominations. But I'm thinking more along the lines of having some denomination which recognizes as many texts as possible which are not in every Biblical canon IOTL (and possible none), e.g. Acts of various specific figures (as distinct from Acts of the Apostles), Gospel of Thomas, etc. etc.

A Christian or post-Christian religion that incorporated as many apocrypha as possible could exist, but it would not simply be “Christianity with a bigger Bible.” It would become a much more plural, mystical, and internally tense tradition unless it created a hierarchy of authority inside its canon.

The closest historical model is the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose biblical canon is among the broadest in Christianity. It includes texts such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and several books not found in Catholic, Protestant, or most Orthodox Bibles. Another partial comparison is Latter-day Saint Christianity, which accepts additional scripture, though not mainly ancient apocrypha. A new “maximal apocryphal” church would go even further than either.

Such a religion would likely include the standard Old and New Testaments, the Catholic and Orthodox deuterocanonical books, the Ethiopian broader canon, Jewish pseudepigrapha such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Life of Adam and Eve, and many apocalypses. It might also canonize New Testament apocrypha: the Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Peter, Infancy Gospel of Thomas, Protoevangelium of James, Acts of Paul and Thecla, Acts of Peter, Apocalypse of Peter, Gospel of Nicodemus, various Marian texts, apostolic acts, and perhaps even Gnostic or quasi-Gnostic works such as the Gospel of Philip, Gospel of Truth, Apocryphon of John, and Pistis Sophia.

The main problem is that these texts do not agree with each other. Some are broadly compatible with ancient Catholic or Orthodox Christianity. Others teach very different views of creation, salvation, Jesus’ body, gender, angels, demons, sexuality, martyrdom, and the nature of God. For example, Enochic literature expands the role of angels, fallen watchers, cosmic judgment, and heavenly journeys. Marian apocrypha elevate Mary and her sacred biography. Infancy gospels depict a wonder-working child Jesus in ways that many Christians find theologically awkward. Gnostic texts often treat the material world as a trap or mistake and distinguish the highest God from the creator, which conflicts sharply with Jewish and orthodox Christian belief in one good Creator.

So the religion would have to choose one of two paths.

If it gave every apocryphal text equal doctrinal authority, the result would be highly unstable. Its theology would be contradictory: creation might be good in one text and a cosmic prison in another; Jesus might be fully incarnate in one text and only seemingly embodied in another; salvation might come through faith, sacraments, martyrdom, asceticism, secret knowledge, or angelic ascent depending on which text was emphasized. Such a church would probably be rejected by mainstream Christians as heretical or post-Christian.

If, however, it used a layered canon, it could be more coherent. It might say: the Gospels and core apostolic writings are primary; the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books are foundational; Enochic, Marian, apostolic, and apocalyptic texts are inspired but secondary; Gnostic or speculative writings are “mystical canon” to be interpreted allegorically rather than literally. This would resemble how some traditions distinguish between canonical scripture, liturgical books, writings of the fathers, and mystical theology, but it would bring many of those texts formally inside the canon.

The resulting religion would probably be strongly apocalyptic, angelological, sacramental, and mystical. It would emphasize hidden histories of heaven and hell, elaborate ranks of angels and demons, visionary ascents, sacred names, the harrowing of hell, Mary’s cosmic role, apostolic legends, and secret teachings of Jesus. It might also become more ascetic, since many apocryphal acts praise celibacy, renunciation, fasting, and martyrdom. Its Jesus would be not only the crucified and risen Messiah but also a revealer of hidden cosmic knowledge.

Institutionally, it would need powerful interpretive authorities: councils, bishops, prophets, scholars, or a magisterium capable of deciding how conflicting scriptures should be read. Without that, the canon would fragment the religion into factions, each favoring different apocrypha.

In short: a maximally apocryphal Christian canon is possible, but it would push the religion toward a broad, esoteric, post-orthodox form of Christianity. It would gain richness, mythic depth, and mystical variety, but at the cost of doctrinal simplicity and compatibility with mainstream Christian tradition.

edus.text: A Christian or post-Christian religion that incorporated as many apocrypha as possible could exist,
but it would not simply be “Christianity with a bigger Bible.”
It would become a much more plural, mystical, and internally tense tradition
unless it created a hierarchy of authority inside its canon.
The closest historical model is the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church,
whose biblical canon is among the broadest in Christianity.
It includes texts such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, and several books not found in Catholic, Protestant, or most Orthodox Bibles.
Another partial comparison is Latter-day Saint Christianity,
which accepts additional scripture,
though not mainly ancient apocrypha.
A new “maximal apocryphal” church would go even further than either.

Such a religion would likely include the standard Old and New Testaments, the Catholic and Orthodox deuterocanonical books, the Ethiopian broader canon, Jewish pseudepigrapha such as 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Life of Adam and Eve, and many apocalypses.

It might also canonize New Testament apocrypha: the Gospel of Thomas, Gospel of Peter, Infancy Gospel of Thomas, Protoevangelium of James, Acts of Paul and Thecla, Acts of Peter, Apocalypse of Peter, Gospel of Nicodemus, various Marian texts, apostolic acts, and perhaps even Gnostic or quasi-Gnostic works such as the Gospel of Philip, Gospel of Truth, Apocryphon of John, and Pistis Sophia.
The main problem is that these texts do not agree with each other.
Some are broadly compatible with ancient Catholic or Orthodox Christianity.
Others teach very different views of creation, salvation, Jesus’ body, gender, angels, demons, sexuality, martyrdom, and the nature of God.
For example, Enochic literature expands the role of angels, fallen watchers, cosmic judgment, and heavenly journeys.
Marian apocrypha elevate Mary and her sacred biography.
Infancy gospels depict a wonder-working child Jesus in ways that many Christians find theologically awkward.

Gnostic texts often treat the material world as a trap or mistake and distinguish the highest God from the creator, which conflicts sharply with Jewish and orthodox Christian belief in one good Creator.
So the religion would have to choose one of two paths.
If it gave every apocryphal text equal doctrinal authority,
the result would be highly unstable.
Its theology would be contradictory:
creation might be good in one text and a cosmic prison in another;
Jesus might be fully incarnate in one text and only seemingly embodied in another;
salvation might come through faith, sacraments, martyrdom, asceticism, secret knowledge, or angelic ascent depending on which text was emphasized.
Such a church would probably be rejected by mainstream Christians as heretical or post-Christian.
If, however, it used a layered canon,
it could be more coherent.
It might say: the Gospels and core apostolic writings are primary;
the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books are foundational;
Enochic, Marian, apostolic, and apocalyptic texts are inspired but secondary;
Gnostic or speculative writings are “mystical canon” to be interpreted allegorically rather than literally.
This would resemble how some traditions distinguish between canonical scripture, liturgical books, writings of the fathers, and mystical theology,
but it would bring many of those texts formally inside the canon.
The resulting religion would probably be strongly apocalyptic, angelological, sacramental, and mystical.

It would emphasize hidden histories of heaven and hell, elaborate ranks of angels and demons, visionary ascents, sacred names, the harrowing of hell, Mary’s cosmic role, apostolic legends, and secret teachings of Jesus.
It might also become more ascetic,
since many apocryphal acts praise celibacy, renunciation, fasting, and martyrdom.
Its Jesus would be not only the crucified and risen Messiah but also a revealer of hidden cosmic knowledge.
Institutionally, it would need powerful interpretive authorities: councils, bishops, prophets, scholars, or a magisterium
capable of deciding how conflicting scriptures should be read.
Without that, the canon would fragment the religion into factions,
each favoring different apocrypha.
In short: a maximally apocryphal Christian canon is possible,
but it would push the religion toward a broad, esoteric, post-orthodox form of Christianity.
It would gain richness, mythic depth, and mystical variety,
but at the cost of doctrinal simplicity and compatibility with mainstream Christian tradition.

human_answers: "What factors allowed the European powers to accept native princes in Serbia" is a false question because it presumes the European powers had a role in allowing native princes there to begin with. With the exception of Russia during the First Serbian Uprising, there were no other powers involved beyond the Ottomans. Had it ended with the First Serbian Uprising, whether in Ičko's Peace in 1807 or by 1813 otherwise, we would've seen the Ottomans consenting to a native prince in the region, in the form of Karađorđe, by themselves, and that'd be the end of it. Karađorđe was already attempting to consolidate power for himself in those latter years, even while he had opposition, so he was already set to be uncontested. Which brings forth two questions: had the Greeks fought alone, would it have increased the odds of a native prince being put in power, and would they have even chosen to be a monarchy? As others have argued so far, there was too much conflict between the various revolutionaries to allow for something like that, and it's also why OTL there actually wasn't a monarchy in Greece after the revolution until Greece's stability was brought under question and it was decided by the Great Powers that it should be a monarchy with a foreign prince in power to bolster it. This ignores some of the historical facts surrounding the dynastic conflict in Serbia. Obrenović didn't just decide he was going to challenge Karađorđe's claim to authority over the Serbs, he had become a leader in his own right, rallied the people to another uprising, and won, by the time Karađorđe attempted to come back. He had received what Karađorđe would've gotten had the First Serbian Uprising won, effectively, and he wasn't going to let him challenge that, least of all because of fears of what the Ottomans might do in response. Had the Greek War of Independence seen a decisively unifying leader like Karađorđe or Obrenović from its outset, there's no reason to assume that you'd have other leaders contesting their claim to power by wishing to assert themselves instead - when Karađorđe attempted to consolidate power, he received pushback on it, and it's likely a Greek-equivalent situation would see a similar conflict, where the consolidating leader would receive pushback from his revolutionary peers. But as everyone else has pointed out, revolutionary leadership was a lot more diffuse and filled with conflict, so there's no chance you'd have a unifying leader like that emerge. Really, the case of Serbia should highlight the fact that, had the Greek War of Independence not been a war for independence, but a war for greater autonomy ala the First Serbian Uprising up to 1807, in a TL where it was successful, depending on who's Sultan at the time, the same privileges extended in Ičko's Peace to the Serbs might be extended to the Greeks too, which means that the Ottomans would've demanded the Greeks decide on who to be prince among their leaders.

AHC: Greek royal family that is ethnically Greek

Greece became independent from the Ottoman Empire in 1821. Two different European dynasties ruled it - the Bavarians (whose only king of Greece was the unpopular King Otto) and the Danish. Neither of these dynasties were of Greek heritage. However, there was a sizable Greek aristocracy in the Ottoman Empire, such as the Phanariotes of Constantinople. What if an ethnically Greek family (such as one of the Phanariot families) was chosen to rule Greece? Can you think of some candidates for a possible ethnically Greek royal family for 19th century Greece?
